A.explanation: Total resistance $R+r$ rises from $10 \, \Omega$ to $55 \, \Omega$, so current $I = E/(R+r)$ falls, not rises.

B.explanation: Lost volts $Ir$ falls because $I$ falls, so terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$ rises from $5.0 \, \text{V}$ toward $10 \, \text{V}$.

C.explanation: With smaller current, $P = I^2 r$ in the $5.0 \, \Omega$ internal resistance decreases.

D.explanation: Total power $P = EI$ decreases because $E = 10 \, \text{V}$ is fixed and $I$ decreases.

hints: Notice the total resistance in series: $5.0 \, \Omega$ internal plus the load, first $5.0 \, \Omega$ then $50 \, \Omega$.
Connect this to current $I = E/(R+r)$ with fixed e.m.f. $E = 10 \, \text{V}$, then to lost volts $Ir$ and terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$.
Compare $V = IR = E \times R/(R+r)$ for $R = 5.0 \, \Omega$ and $R = 50 \, \Omega$ to see which share of the 10 V goes to the load.
walkthrough: Identify the series circuit: e.m.f. $E = 10 \, \text{V}$, internal resistance $r = 5.0 \, \Omega$, load $R = 5.0 \, \Omega$ then $50 \, \Omega$.
State the current rule $I = E/(R+r)$. Initially $I_1 = 10/(5.0+5.0) = 1.0 \, \text{A}$. Finally $I_2 = 10/(50+5.0) = 10/55 \approx 0.18 \, \text{A}$, so current decreases.

State the load p.d. rule $V = IR = E - Ir$. Initially $V_1 = 1.0 \times 5.0 = 5.0 \, \text{V}$. Finally $V_2 = 0.18 \times 50 \approx 9.1 \, \text{V}$, so load p.d. increases as lost volts $Ir$ falls.
Check power: internal $I^2r$ falls from $5.0 \, \text{W}$ to about $0.17 \, \text{W}$, and total $EI$ falls from $10 \, \text{W}$ to about $1.8 \, \text{W}$.
Only the increase in potential difference across the load matches the calculation. This is option B.
